guides.title: Association Football Rules and Positions
guides.summary: A complete account of how association football is governed and played: the seventeen Laws of the Game, the field and equipment, offside, fouls and restarts, and the positional roles and formations that organise eleven players into a team.

sections.heading: What the Game Is and Who Writes the Rules
sections.body:
Association football is a game played between two teams of eleven players who attempt to put a ball into the opposing team's goal without using their hands or arms, with the sole exception of each team's goalkeeper inside a marked area near their own goal. It is the most widely played and watched sport in the world, and part of the reason is that its rulebook is short, stable and expressed in ordinary language. The entire code fits into seventeen numbered Laws, and those Laws have changed only incrementally since they were first written down. A person who understands the seventeen Laws can walk onto a pitch anywhere on earth and play. 

The rules were codified in London on 26 October 1863, when representatives of a dozen clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern to found the Football Association and agree a single set of Laws. Before that meeting, almost every school and town played a different game: the Cambridge Rules of the 1840s and the Sheffield Rules of 1858 were serious attempts at codification, but they disagreed with each other and with everyone else about handling, hacking the shins, and offside. The 1863 meeting settled the central question by voting to forbid carrying the ball in the hands and to forbid hacking, at which point the clubs that wanted those things left and eventually formed the separate code of rugby football. The word soccer is simply a nineteenth-century English slang abbreviation of the word association, formed the same way rugby football became rugger. 

Since 1886 the Laws have been owned not by any national federation but by the International Football Association Board, universally called the IFAB. It was created so that England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland could agree on a common code, and it retains an unusual constitution. The IFAB has eight votes: four belong to FIFA, the world governing body founded in 1904, and one each to the English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish associations. Any change to the Laws requires six of those eight votes, which means FIFA cannot change the Laws alone and neither can the four British associations acting together. That deliberately awkward arithmetic is why the game has resisted the constant rule-tinkering common in other sports. 

The Laws are also written to be applied by a human being in real time with no equipment beyond a whistle, and they say so explicitly. Many of them turn on judgements of intent, carelessness and interference that no mechanical test could settle. A referee is instructed to use the Laws to make the game safe, fair and enjoyable, and is given discretion to let trivial infringements go. Understanding football's rules therefore means understanding both the written text and the conventions of interpretation that referees are trained to apply, because the two together are what actually governs a match.

sections.heading: The Field of Play and Its Markings
sections.body:
A football pitch is a rectangle of grass or approved artificial turf whose dimensions are given as ranges rather than fixed numbers, which is unusual among major sports and has real tactical consequences. The touchline, running the long way, must be between 90 and 120 metres (100 to 130 yards). The goal line, running the short way behind each goal, must be between 45 and 90 metres (50 to 100 yards). The touchline must always be longer than the goal line. For matches between national teams the ranges narrow considerably: 100 to 110 metres long by 64 to 75 metres wide, which is why international pitches feel more uniform than club pitches. A common professional size is 105 by 68 metres. All lines are part of the areas they bound, and they must be of the same width, no more than 12 centimetres. 

The pitch is divided in half by a halfway line with a centre mark at its midpoint, around which a circle of 9.15 metres (10 yards) radius is drawn. That radius, ten yards, recurs throughout the Laws as the standard distance opponents must retreat at a restart. Each goal sits centred on its goal line and consists of two upright posts 7.32 metres (8 yards) apart joined by a horizontal crossbar 2.44 metres (8 feet) above the ground. Posts and crossbar must be white, of the same width and depth as the goal line, and no more than 12 centimetres thick, and they must be anchored securely, a requirement written in blood after portable goals have fallen on and killed children. 

Two nested rectangles sit in front of each goal. The goal area, often called the six-yard box, extends 5.5 metres from the inside of each post and 5.5 metres into the field. The penalty area, the eighteen-yard box, extends 16.5 metres from the inside of each post and 16.5 metres into the field. Inside the penalty area a penalty mark is placed 11 metres (12 yards) from the midpoint between the posts, and outside the area an arc of 9.15 metres radius is drawn around that mark so that players know where they may not stand during a penalty kick. The penalty area is legally decisive: it defines where the goalkeeper may handle the ball and where a direct free kick offence becomes a penalty kick. 

At each corner stands a flagpost at least 1.5 metres high with a non-pointed top, and a quarter circle of one metre radius is drawn inside the field from it. Optional marks 9.15 metres from the corner arc may be made outside the goal line and touchline to help referees judge the retreat distance at corner kicks. A technical area for each team's coaching staff, and the width of the goal nets if used, are governed by competition rules rather than by the Laws themselves.

sections.heading: The Ball, the Players and the Equipment
sections.body:
The ball must be spherical, made of suitable material, between 68 and 70 centimetres in circumference, and between 410 and 450 grams in weight at the start of the match. Its pressure must be between 0.6 and 1.1 atmospheres at sea level, which is 600 to 1,100 grams per square centimetre, or roughly 8.5 to 15.6 pounds per square inch. Those tolerances matter more than they look. A ball inflated to the top of the range is harder, flies further and skids off wet grass; a soft ball dies on the first touch and rewards close control. The mass range is why a wet, muddy leather ball of the pre-1960s era, which absorbed water and could gain hundreds of grams over ninety minutes, was a genuinely different and more dangerous object to head than a modern coated synthetic one. 

A match is played by two teams of not more than eleven players, one of whom must be the goalkeeper. A match may not start, and must be abandoned if it has started, if either team has fewer than seven players on the field. That threshold, seven, is a practical compromise: it permits a team reduced by injuries and dismissals to continue but stops matches becoming farcical. Substitutions are governed by competition rules within limits set by the Laws. Most senior competitions now allow five substitutions, a change introduced as a temporary measure during the compressed fixture calendar of 2020 and written permanently into the Laws in 2022, with the restriction that they be made in a maximum of three stoppages plus half-time so that a team cannot break up play repeatedly. Additional permanent concussion substitutes are permitted in many competitions and do not count against that total. 

Compulsory equipment is a shirt with sleeves, shorts, socks, shinguards and footwear. Shinguards must be covered entirely by the socks, made of a suitable material, and provide reasonable protection: a bare tibia struck by a studded boot fractures readily, and this is the one piece of protective equipment the Laws insist on. The two teams must wear colours distinguishing them from each other, from the match officials and, in the goalkeepers' case, from all outfield players. Undershorts and undershirts, if worn, must match the main colour of the corresponding garment. 

Jewellery of every kind is forbidden, including rings, necklaces, earrings and hair beads, and taping over them is not sufficient. Any other equipment, such as headgear, face masks, knee braces or spectacles, is permitted only if it is not dangerous and has been inspected by the referee. Modern electronic performance and tracking systems, the vests containing GPS units that players wear beneath their shirts, are explicitly allowed provided they are not dangerous and, in official competitions, are approved to the relevant standard.

sections.heading: The Officials and Video Assistance
sections.body:
Every match is controlled by a referee who has full authority to enforce the Laws in connection with the match, and whose decisions regarding facts connected with play are final. That phrase is doing heavy work: it means a referee's judgement that a ball crossed a line, or that a challenge was careless, cannot be overturned by protest, and it is the reason football has historically absorbed obvious errors rather than replaying matches. A referee may change a decision only on realising it is incorrect or on the advice of another official, and only if play has not restarted or the match has not been ended. 

The referee is normally assisted by two assistant referees, one on each touchline, who patrol the halves nearest their own bench and signal when the ball leaves the field, which team is entitled to the restart, whether a player is in an offside position, and offences they see that the referee could not. The assistant on the far side from an incident often has the only clear view. A fourth official manages substitutions and the technical areas and indicates the minimum additional time. Larger competitions may add two additional assistant referees positioned behind each goal, and reserve assistant referees. 

Two technologies have been admitted into the Laws. Goal-line technology, permitted from 2012, determines automatically and within one second whether the whole of the ball has crossed the whole of the goal line, signalling to the referee's watch. It is a purely factual, binary determination, which is why it has been uncontroversial. The video assistant referee, or VAR, was written into the Laws in 2018 and is far more contested because it applies to judgement calls. VAR may intervene in only four categories of decision: goals and the offences leading up to them, penalty decisions and the offences leading up to them, direct red card incidents, and mistaken identity when a card is shown to the wrong player. 

The threshold for VAR intervention is a clear and obvious error, or a serious missed incident. The video official does not re-referee the match; the on-field referee remains the decision-maker and, for subjective calls, is expected to view the replay personally at a pitchside monitor before changing a decision. Factual matters such as whether an offside player was ahead of the second-last defender, or whether a foul occurred inside or outside the penalty area, are treated as objective and may be corrected without an on-field review. The persistent criticism of VAR is not that it is wrong more often than the naked eye but that drawing millimetre offside lines on a moving image imposes a precision the underlying evidence does not support, and that long delays damage the rhythm of a game whose appeal rests on continuous play. Semi-automated offside systems using limb tracking were introduced from 2022 partly to shorten those delays.

sections.heading: Duration, Kick-Off and Ball In and Out of Play
sections.body:
A match lasts two equal halves of 45 minutes, reduced only by agreement between the referee and the two teams before the start and only if competition rules permit. The half-time interval must not exceed 15 minutes. Time is kept by the referee, not by a stadium clock, and the clock does not stop. Instead the referee adds an allowance at the end of each half for time lost through substitutions, injuries and their treatment, time-wasting, disciplinary sanctions, drinks breaks, VAR reviews, and any other cause including significant delays at a restart such as goal celebrations. The fourth official indicates the minimum amount to be added, and the referee may add more but never less. A directive applied at the 2022 World Cup produced added times of eight and ten minutes and showed how much of the nominal ninety had been lost. 

A coin toss decides which team chooses which goal to attack in the first half; the other team takes the kick-off. In the second half the teams change ends and the team that won the toss takes the kick-off. At a kick-off all players except the kicker must be in their own half, opponents must be at least 9.15 metres from the ball until it is in play, and the ball must be stationary on the centre mark. Since 2016 the ball is in play as soon as it is kicked and clearly moves, and it may be kicked in any direction, which ended the century-old convention of a mandatory forward touch to a second player. A goal may be scored directly from a kick-off, and if it goes directly into the kicker's own goal a corner is awarded. 

The ball is out of play when it has wholly crossed the goal line or touchline on the ground or in the air, or when play has been stopped by the referee, or when it touches a match official, remains on the field and a promising attack or a change of possession or a goal results. Crucially, the whole of the ball must cross the whole of the line. A ball overhanging the line, however far, is still in play, which is why goal-line technology exists and why an assistant referee standing level with the line is essential. At all other times the ball is in play, including when it rebounds off a goalpost, crossbar, corner flagpost or a match official and stays on the field. 

If play is stopped for a reason not covered by another Law, or the ball touches an official in the circumstances listed, the restart is a dropped ball. Since 2019 the dropped ball is no longer contested: it is given to the goalkeeper in their own penalty area if the stoppage occurred there, and otherwise to the one player of the team that last touched the ball, at the point of the last touch, with all other players of both teams at least four metres away until it is in play. That change removed the manufactured scramble and the awkward etiquette of deliberately returning the ball after a stoppage.

sections.heading: Scoring, Results and Ways of Deciding a Tie
sections.body:
A goal is scored when the whole of the ball passes over the whole of the goal line between the goalposts and beneath the crossbar, provided that no offence has been committed by the scoring team beforehand. The team scoring the greater number of goals wins; if both score the same number, or neither scores, the match is drawn. Nothing else counts. Football has no partial scores, no points for near misses and no reward for territorial dominance, which is the structural reason it produces more upsets than higher-scoring sports: a typical professional match yields fewer than three goals in total, so a single deflection carries an enormous share of the outcome. 

There is one important prohibition. A goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in; if the ball goes into the opponents' goal a goal kick is awarded, and if into the thrower's own goal a corner kick is awarded to the opponents. A goal may be scored directly from a kick-off, a goal kick, a corner kick, a free kick or a drop kick, but never from a dropped ball, which if it enters a goal untouched by a second player is restarted with a goal kick or a corner kick as appropriate. 

When a competition needs a winner from a drawn match, the Laws recognise three permitted procedures, chosen by competition rules. Away goals, under which the team scoring more goals away from home over a two-legged tie advances, was used for decades and has been progressively abandoned since the early 2020s on the grounds that travel and pitch conditions no longer justify it. Extra time consists of two further equal periods of not more than 15 minutes each, with a short drinks interval but no proper break between them, and an additional substitution is normally permitted. The golden goal and silver goal experiments of the late 1990s, in which the first goal in extra time ended the match, were tried at major tournaments and then discarded because they encouraged extreme caution. 

The final resort is kicks from the penalty mark, commonly called a penalty shoot-out, which is formally not part of the match and whose goals are not added to the score. Both teams take five kicks alternately unless one establishes a lead the other cannot reach. If still level, the same procedure continues one pair of kicks at a time until one team scores and the other does not. Only players on the field at the end of play may take part, and before a player takes a second kick every eligible player on that team must have taken one. If one team ends the match with more players than the other, the larger team must reduce to equate, a rule that prevents a dismissal from becoming an advantage. The referee tosses a coin for the goal to be used, and a second toss decides which team kicks first; since 2017 the team winning that toss may choose to go first or second.

sections.heading: The Offside Law
sections.body:
Offside, Law 11, is the single rule that gives football its shape, and it is the one most often misunderstood, because it is really two separate tests applied at two separate moments. The first test asks about position. A player is in an offside position if any part of the head, body or feet is in the opponents' half, not counting the halfway line itself, and is nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. Hands and arms are excluded from the measurement up to the bottom of the armpit, because those parts cannot legally score. The second-last opponent is usually the last outfield defender with the goalkeeper behind, but not always: if the goalkeeper has advanced, the second-last opponent may be an outfield player. Being level with the second-last opponent, or level with the last two opponents, is not an offside position. 

The second test asks about involvement, and it is judged at the exact moment a teammate plays or touches the ball, not at the moment the offside player receives it. Being in an offside position is not in itself an offence. It becomes an offence only if, at that moment, the player becomes involved in active play in one of three ways: by interfering with play, meaning playing or touching the ball passed or touched by a teammate; by interfering with an opponent, which covers preventing an opponent playing the ball by clearly obstructing their line of vision, challenging for the ball, making an obvious action that clearly impacts an opponent, or making an obvious attempt to play a ball close by that impacts an opponent; or by gaining an advantage from a ball that has rebounded or been deflected off a goalpost, crossbar, match official or opponent, or from a deliberate save. 

Two categories of contact by a defender reset the situation. If a defender deliberately plays the ball, other than a deliberate save, a player in an offside position is no longer penalised for receiving it. If a defender merely deflects the ball, or makes a deliberate save, the offside offence stands. The distinction between a deliberate play and a deflection turns on whether the defender had control of the option and time to make a considered action, and it is genuinely one of the hardest judgements in the game. 

There is no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from a goal kick, a corner kick or a throw-in, and no offside in a player's own half. The free kick for an offside offence is indirect and is taken from the place where the offence occurred, including inside the offending player's own half. The Law's history is instructive: until 1925 three opponents had to be nearer the goal line, and reducing that number to two produced an immediate scoring explosion, from about 4,700 goals in the English First Division in 1924 to 25 to more than 6,300 the following season, and it forced the tactical invention of the centre-back.

sections.heading: Fouls: Direct and Indirect Free Kicks
sections.body:
Law 12 divides offences into those punished by a direct free kick, from which a goal may be scored immediately, and those punished by an indirect free kick, from which the ball must touch another player before a goal counts. The distinction matters enormously in and around the penalty area, because a direct free kick offence committed by a defender inside their own penalty area is punished by a penalty kick, while an indirect free kick offence there is not. 

A direct free kick is awarded when a player commits any of seven physical offences against an opponent in a manner the referee considers careless, reckless or using excessive force: charging, jumping at, kicking or attempting to kick, pushing, striking or attempting to strike including head-butting, tackling or challenging, and tripping or attempting to trip. Careless means showing a lack of attention or consideration, and carries no disciplinary sanction. Reckless means acting with disregard to the danger to, or consequences for, an opponent, and must be cautioned with a yellow card. Using excessive force means exceeding the necessary use of force and endangering the safety of an opponent, and must be punished by dismissal. These three gradations are the spine of football's disciplinary system and are worth memorising, because almost every argument about a challenge is really an argument about which of the three applies. 

A direct free kick is also awarded for holding, impeding an opponent with contact, biting or spitting at anyone, throwing an object at the ball, an opponent or an official, and for handling the ball. The handball Law was substantially rewritten between 2019 and 2021 and now turns on three ideas: a deliberate act of moving the hand or arm towards the ball; making the body unnaturally bigger by having the arm above shoulder height or extended beyond a position justified by the body's movement; and scoring directly from the hand or arm, or immediately after the ball has touched the scorer's own hand or arm, which is an offence even when entirely accidental. Accidental contact by a teammate in the build-up is no longer an offence, a correction made in 2021 after the earlier text produced widely disliked disallowed goals. 

Indirect free kicks cover playing in a dangerous manner without contact, such as a high boot near a lowered head; impeding the progress of an opponent without contact; dissent, offensive language and other verbal offences; preventing the goalkeeper releasing the ball from the hands; and a set of goalkeeper-specific offences. All free kicks are taken from where the offence occurred, with opponents at least 9.15 metres away until the ball is in play, and since 2019 attacking players must stay at least one metre from a defensive wall of three or more players. A free kick to the defending team inside its own penalty area is in play as soon as it is kicked and clearly moves, and opponents must be outside the area until then.

sections.heading: Cautions, Dismissals and Disciplinary Sanctions
sections.body:
Football's disciplinary vocabulary is two coloured cards, introduced by the English referee Ken Aston, who reportedly conceived them while stopped at traffic lights after a 1966 World Cup quarter-final in which two Argentine players had not understood they were being sent off. They were used at the 1970 World Cup and have been universal since. A yellow card is a caution; a red card is a dismissal, and a dismissed player must leave the field and its surroundings and cannot be replaced, so the team plays short for the remainder of the match. Two cautions in the same match produce a second yellow and an automatic red. 

The cautionable offences are a closed list worth knowing precisely: delaying the restart of play; dissent by word or action; entering, re-entering or deliberately leaving the field without the referee's permission; failing to respect the required distance at a corner kick, free kick or throw-in; persistent offences, with no fixed number specified; and unsporting behaviour, which is the broad category covering shirt-pulling to stop an attack, simulation, handling to stop a promising attack, and excessive celebration such as removing the shirt or climbing a perimeter fence. A player who is cautioned or sent off before entering the field, or after leaving it, is still liable, and offences committed off the field against anyone including officials and spectators are punishable. 

The sending-off offences are likewise a closed list: denying the opposing team a goal or an obvious goal-scoring opportunity by a deliberate handball, other than by a goalkeeper in their own penalty area; denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity to an opponent moving towards the goal by an offence punishable by a free kick; serious foul play; biting or spitting at someone; violent conduct; using offensive, insulting or abusive language or gestures; and receiving a second caution. Serious foul play means a challenge that endangers an opponent's safety or uses excessive force while contesting the ball; violent conduct is force or brutality used when not contesting the ball, and can be committed against a teammate, an official or a spectator. 

Assessing an obvious goal-scoring opportunity, universally abbreviated to DOGSO, follows four published considerations: the distance between the offence and the goal, the general direction of play, the likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball, and the location and number of defenders. Since 2016 the so-called triple punishment has been mitigated: if the offence is an attempt to play the ball and occurs inside the offender's penalty area, the penalty kick already restores the goal-scoring chance, so the player is cautioned rather than sent off. Holding, pulling, pushing, no attempt to play the ball, or an offence punishable by a red card regardless of position still means dismissal. Suspensions following a red card are set by competition rules, not by the Laws, and commonly run from one match for a second caution to three or more for violent conduct.

sections.heading: Restarts: Throw-Ins, Goal Kicks, Corner Kicks and Advantage
sections.body:
When the ball wholly crosses a touchline the restart is a throw-in, awarded to the opponents of the player who last touched it. The technique is prescribed with unusual specificity because it would otherwise become a throwing contest: the thrower must face the field, have part of each foot on the touchline or on the ground outside it, hold the ball with both hands, and deliver it from behind and over the head from the point where it left the field. All opponents must stand at least two metres from the point of the throw. The thrower may not touch the ball again until it has touched another player, and a goal cannot be scored directly. There is no offside from a throw-in, which is why long throws into the penalty area became a specialist weapon. 

When the ball wholly crosses the goal line having last touched a player of the attacking team, and a goal is not scored, the restart is a goal kick, taken from anywhere within the goal area by any player of the defending team. The 2019 revision was significant: the ball is now in play as soon as it is kicked and clearly moves, and it no longer has to leave the penalty area. Opponents must remain outside the penalty area until then, but a team may legally pass the ball to a defender standing inside its own six-yard box. That single change did more to reshape modern build-up play than any other recent amendment, because it let goalkeepers begin attacks from the edge of the goal area against a high press. 

When the ball wholly crosses the goal line having last touched a player of the defending team, the restart is a corner kick from within the corner arc nearest where it crossed. The flagpost must not be moved, opponents must be at least 9.15 metres from the arc until the ball is in play, and a goal may be scored directly, including against the kicker's own team, in which case a corner is awarded to the opponents. As with all restarts the kicker may not play the ball a second time until someone else has touched it. 

The most consequential piece of refereeing discretion is not a restart at all but the advantage clause. The referee may allow play to continue when an offence has occurred if the offended team would benefit more from the continuation, and may return to and penalise the original offence if the anticipated advantage does not materialise within a few seconds. Signalling advantage does not cancel any disciplinary sanction: a reckless challenge still earns its yellow card at the next stoppage, and an offence that denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity but from which a goal is nevertheless scored is reduced to a caution. Judging advantage well is what separates competent from good referees, because stopping a flowing attack to award a free kick thirty metres further back punishes the wronged team twice.

sections.heading: The Penalty Kick and the Goalkeeper's Duel
sections.body:
A penalty kick is awarded when a player commits a direct free kick offence inside their own penalty area, or off the field as part of play, while the ball is in play. It is the single most valuable set piece in the sport: conversion rates in senior professional football sit at roughly three in four, and have been remarkably stable at that level for decades, which means a penalty is worth about 0.75 of a goal against an open-play shot worth perhaps a tenth of that. 

The ball is placed on the penalty mark, 11 metres from the goal line. The kicker must be clearly identified. The defending goalkeeper must remain on the goal line facing the kicker, between the posts, without touching the goalposts, crossbar or net, and at the moment the kick is taken must have at least part of one foot touching, in line with, or behind the goal line. That wording, adopted in 2019, deliberately relaxed the old requirement that both feet stay on the line, acknowledging that goalkeepers naturally move as they dive. Every other player must be on the field, outside the penalty area, behind the penalty mark, and at least 9.15 metres from it, which is the purpose of the arc drawn outside the area. 

The kicker must kick the ball forward, may use a backheel provided the ball travels forward, and may not touch it again until another player has. Feinting in the run-up is permitted; feinting after completing the run-up is an offence, punished by a caution and an indirect free kick to the defending team even if a goal results. If the goalkeeper offends and the kick is missed or saved, the kick is retaken and the goalkeeper is warned for a first offence and cautioned for repeats; if the goalkeeper offends and a goal is scored, the goal stands. If an attacking teammate encroaches and a goal is scored, the kick is retaken; if a defending teammate encroaches and the kick is missed, it is retaken. If both teams encroach, the kick is retaken regardless of outcome. 

Tactically the penalty is a game of commitment under time pressure. A well-struck ball travels the 11 metres in roughly 0.4 to 0.5 seconds, and a goalkeeper needs about 0.6 seconds to move from a standing start to a post, so a keeper who waits until the ball is struck cannot reach the corners. The consequence is that keepers must anticipate, and kickers face a choice between a placed shot into a corner, which a guessing keeper may reach, and a hard shot down the middle, which succeeds only if the keeper has already committed. Goalkeepers who delay their dive, sometimes called staying big, force the kicker to aim precisely and are the reason the modern technique of waiting for the keeper to move, the so-called paradinha or stutter, is so tightly regulated.

sections.heading: The Goalkeeper: Special Rights and Restrictions
sections.body:
The goalkeeper is the only player permitted to handle the ball, and that permission is bounded in space and time. Handling is allowed only inside the goalkeeper's own penalty area and only while the ball is in play. Outside the area the goalkeeper is an ordinary outfield player, and handling there is a direct free kick offence, punished by dismissal if it denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity. The goalkeeper must wear colours distinguishable from both teams' outfield players and from the match officials, and may change places with any outfield player during a stoppage provided the referee is informed. 

Three restrictions define the modern goalkeeper's game, and all three exist to stop time-wasting. The first is the back-pass rule, introduced in 1992 after the notoriously defensive 1990 World Cup: the goalkeeper commits an indirect free kick offence by touching the ball with the hands after it has been deliberately kicked to them by a teammate, or after receiving it directly from a teammate's throw-in. A ball headed, chested or kneed back is legal, and so is a genuine deflection, but a deliberate flick with the foot is not, and referees are instructed to judge whether the teammate deliberately kicked rather than whether they intended to pass. This one amendment transformed goalkeeping from a specialist shot-stopping trade into a footballing position and is the root of the modern sweeper-keeper. 

The second restriction concerns holding the ball. For decades a goalkeeper who controlled the ball with the hands for more than six seconds conceded an indirect free kick, a sanction so severe that referees almost never gave it, leaving the rule effectively dead. For the 2025/26 season the IFAB replaced it with an eight-second limit enforced by a corner kick to the opposing team, with the referee counting down visibly with a raised hand from five. The proportionate punishment was the whole point: a corner is a real but survivable cost, so referees can be expected to apply it. The third restriction is that once the goalkeeper has released the ball from the hands into play they may not touch it again with the hands before another player touches it. 

Beyond the Laws, goalkeeping has a technical grammar of its own. Positioning is governed by narrowing the angle: by advancing along the bisector of the angle formed by the shooter and the two posts, a keeper reduces the visible target area without leaving either post exposed, which is why keepers rush out at a one-on-one rather than waiting on the line. Handling technique distinguishes the W or contour catch for balls above the chest from the scoop or cradle below it, and modern coaching emphasises the set position, a small pre-shot hop that loads the legs so the keeper is neither flat-footed nor airborne when the ball is struck. Distribution is now a first skill rather than an afterthought, and a goalkeeper unable to receive under pressure with the feet is unusable in a possession system.

sections.heading: Defenders and the Back Line
sections.body:
Nothing in the Laws mentions defenders, midfielders or forwards. Positions are entirely a matter of convention and tactics, and any of the ten outfield players may stand anywhere at any time. What creates positions is the offside law, which rewards a defence that holds a straight line, and the simple geometry of a rectangle in which the goal must be protected and the ball must be advanced. The back line is the group nearest one's own goal, normally three or four players, whose primary job is to prevent shots and whose secondary job, in the modern game, is to begin possession. 

Centre-backs, traditionally two, occupy the middle. Their core skills are reading the flight of a ball to attack it in the air, timing a tackle or an interception without conceding a foul in a zone where fouls become penalties, and holding a defensive line in step with a partner so that attackers are caught offside. Historic variations survive in the vocabulary. The stopper marks the opposing centre-forward tightly and contests every ball; the cover or sweeper plays a few metres deeper with no marking assignment, cleaning up balls that get through. The Italian libero of the catenaccio era, and later the ball-playing libero epitomised by Franz Beckenbauer, was a sweeper licensed to carry the ball into midfield. Zonal defending, in which each defender is responsible for a space rather than a person, has largely displaced strict man-marking in open play, though hybrid schemes are normal at set pieces. 

Full-backs occupy the flanks. Historically defensive, they became the most transformed position in the game because a four-man defence facing two forwards has two spare players, and the spare players are the wide ones. A modern full-back is expected to defend one-against-one against a winger, overlap outside that winger to provide width, deliver crosses, and increasingly to invert, stepping into central midfield during possession to create a numerical advantage in the middle while the centre-backs spread. A wing-back is the same player in a back three, occupying the whole flank alone and covering perhaps ten kilometres a match, which is why wing-back is among the most physically demanding roles on the field. 

The back line's collective behaviour matters more than any individual's. A defence that steps up together compresses the space between itself and the midfield, denying the opposition room to receive between the lines and pushing the offside trap higher up the field, but it exposes the space behind to a ball played over the top and demands a goalkeeper willing to sweep outside the penalty area. A defence that drops deep removes the space behind but concedes territory, invites pressure and hands the opposition an easy platform to cross from. Choosing where the line sits is the single most consequential defensive decision a coach makes, and it is constrained by the recovery speed of the slowest centre-back.

sections.heading: Midfield Roles
sections.body:
Midfield is where a match is usually decided, because it is the only region of the pitch that both teams must pass through and the only one where possession can be won far enough from goal to be turned immediately into an attack. A midfield unit has three continuous obligations that pull against one another: screening the space in front of the defence, circulating the ball to keep possession, and arriving in the penalty area to support the attack. No single player can do all three at once, so midfields are built as complementary sets. 

The holding midfielder, often called the six after the continental shirt number, plays closest to the defence. Their job is positional rather than athletic: to occupy the space between the opposition's forwards and midfield, to intercept passes intended for an opposing attacking midfielder, to make the first covering run when a full-back advances, and to offer a safe passing angle so that centre-backs under pressure always have an out. A destroyer version of the role prioritises tackling and duels; a deep-lying playmaker version, the Italian regista, prioritises long, accurate distribution and dictates tempo from that deep position. Two holders side by side, a double pivot, give a team more stability and let one advance while the other covers. 

The central or box-to-box midfielder, the eight, links the two halves of the pitch by covering ground vertically and is judged on the timing of runs beyond the striker and the ability to press an opponent immediately after losing the ball. The attacking midfielder, the ten or trequartista, plays between the opposition's midfield and defence in the zone traditionally called the hole, receiving on the half-turn with defenders behind them and defenders in front. That zone has been squeezed by modern compact defending, which is why the classic number ten is often now deployed wide or as a second striker. 

Wide midfielders differ from wingers mainly in defensive obligation. In a flat four-man midfield the wide players are expected to track opposing full-backs the length of the pitch; in a front three they are attackers who press but rarely retreat to their own penalty area. The inverted winger, a left-footed player on the right or the reverse, is a deliberate choice: cutting inside onto the stronger foot opens the shot at the far post and drags a full-back infield, at the cost of the natural crossing angle an orthodox winger provides. Pressing systems have added a further specification to every midfield role, namely the trigger, the cue such as a backwards pass or a heavy touch that tells the whole unit to move forward together, since an uncoordinated press by one player leaves a hole behind them and is worse than no press at all.

sections.heading: Forwards, Wingers and the Numbering Tradition
sections.body:
Forwards are judged on a harsher and narrower standard than any other position, because their contribution is measured in goals and goals are rare. A striker who scores in one match in three is considered excellent, which means that the difference between a very good and an ordinary forward across a season may be ten goals in perhaps a hundred and twenty shots. The centre-forward's traditional job is to occupy the two centre-backs, attack crosses, and finish chances inside the penalty area, but the modern requirement adds pressing the opposing centre-backs and goalkeeper, since the forward is the first defender in any high press. 

Several distinct archetypes persist. The target man is tall and strong, holds the ball with his back to goal until support arrives, and wins aerial duels from long balls. The poacher or fox in the box plays almost exclusively inside the penalty area, specialising in the half-second of anticipation that turns a rebound into a goal. The complete forward combines hold-up play, movement in behind and finishing. The false nine is the most interesting variation: a nominal centre-forward who drops into midfield instead of occupying the defenders, creating a dilemma because a centre-back who follows leaves a hole for a winger to run into and one who does not concedes a free man in midfield. It was used by Matthias Sindelar's Austrian Wunderteam in the 1930s and by Nándor Hidegkuti for Hungary in the famous 6 to 3 defeat of England at Wembley in 1953, then revived by Pep Guardiola with Lionel Messi at Barcelona from 2009. 

Wingers attack from wide positions and exist because the offside law does not restrain lateral movement and because a defence stretched across the full 68 metres cannot stay compact. An orthodox winger takes on the full-back on the outside and crosses; an inside forward comes infield to shoot or combine; a wide forward in a front three does both depending on which side the ball is. The second striker, sometimes written as the number nine and a half, plays just behind the centre-forward and shares the traits of a ten and a poacher. 

Shirt numbers encode all of this historically. The British convention, fixed when numbering was introduced in the 1920s and made compulsory in 1939, ran 1 goalkeeper, 2 right-back, 3 left-back, 4 right-half, 5 centre-half, 6 left-half, 7 outside-right, 8 inside-right, 9 centre-forward, 10 inside-left, 11 outside-left, mapping the old 2-3-5 pyramid read left to right and back to front. Continental and South American traditions numbered differently, which is why in Britain a 5 usually means a centre-back and a 6 a defensive midfielder, while in the Netherlands, Italy and Argentina a 4 is a centre-back and a 5 or 6 the holding midfielder. Squad numbering, in which a player keeps one number for a season, was adopted in the Premier League in 1993 and severed the last formal link between number and position, but the vocabulary survives everywhere.

sections.heading: Formations, Their Weaknesses and What to Do When Things Go Wrong
sections.body:
A formation is shorthand for the starting distribution of ten outfield players, written from defence forwards, and it is always an approximation because a team's shape in possession differs from its shape out of possession. The first widely used system was the 2-3-5 pyramid of the 1880s, which made sense when three opponents were required to be nearer the goal line for offside. The 1925 reduction to two opponents made the pyramid indefensible, and Herbert Chapman at Arsenal answered by withdrawing the centre-half into defence to create the WM, a 3-2-2-3 that dominated for thirty years. Hungary's 1953 side and Brazil's 4-2-4 of 1958 pushed a fourth defender back, producing the flat back four that has been standard ever since. Helenio Herrera's catenaccio at Internazionale in the 1960s added a sweeper behind man-markers; Rinus Michels' Total Football at Ajax and with the Netherlands in the 1970s made positions interchangeable and used an aggressive offside line as an attacking weapon. The dominant modern shapes are 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 4-4-2 and variants of a back three such as 3-5-2 and 3-4-3. 

Every shape has a structural weakness that follows from arithmetic. A 4-4-2 is balanced and easy to coach but fields two central midfielders against a three and is routinely outnumbered in the middle. A 4-2-3-1 secures the centre but leaves a lone striker isolated when the ball is turned over. A back three is strong against two strikers and against crosses but can be pinned by a front three that occupies all three defenders, and its wing-backs are exposed if the midfield does not cover behind them. A high pressing system concedes the ball over the top; a deep block concedes territory and shots from distance. There is no shape without a cost, and coaching consists largely of deciding which cost to accept. 

When a plan is failing in a match, the reliable diagnostic questions are few. Where is the opposition's free player, and can a shift of one player remove them? Is the team losing the ball in the same place repeatedly, which usually indicates a missing passing angle rather than a bad passer? Are the lines too far apart, letting opponents receive between them? Is the team conceding the same type of chance, such as crosses from one flank or balls in behind a slow centre-back? Changes should be small and specific: pushing one midfielder higher to mark a deep-lying playmaker, dropping the defensive line five metres, switching a winger to the other flank to attack a weaker full-back. 

For a player or a referee arriving new, the most common misunderstandings are worth naming plainly. Offside is judged when the ball is played, not when it is received. A player level with the second-last opponent is onside. Handball is not automatic on any arm contact. A goal from a throw-in does not count. The whole ball must cross the whole line. And a team reduced to fewer than seven players cannot continue. Almost every touchline argument in amateur football turns on one of those six points.

guides.title: How Offside Works in Football
guides.summary: A complete explanation of Law 11 of association football: what an offside position is, when it becomes an offence, the exemptions and rebound rules, the history from 1863 to semi-automated technology, and why the decision is so hard to make with the naked eye.

sections.heading: Why the Law Exists At All
sections.body:
Offside is the only law in association football that most spectators cannot state accurately, and it is also the law without which the sport would not be recognisable. Understanding why it exists is the fastest route to understanding how it works, because every clause in the modern wording is an answer to a specific problem that arose when an earlier version was exploited.

The problem the law solves is goal-hanging. Imagine football with no offside rule. A team could station one or two players permanently beside the opposing goalkeeper, ten yards from the goal, and simply launch long balls forward. Defenders would be obliged to leave players back to mark them, who would in turn require the other side to leave players back, and the game would separate into two disconnected clusters of players camped near each goal with a thinly populated no-man's-land between them. The passing, the collective movement up and down the pitch, and the compressed field on which almost all skilful football happens would disappear. Every code of football that has ever existed has needed some device to prevent this. Rugby solves it by forbidding the forward pass entirely. Ice hockey uses a blue line. Basketball uses a shot clock and a restricted area. Association football uses offside.

What the law does, in effect, is impose a moving boundary. An attacker may not receive the ball ahead of the second-rearmost defender: the defence, by moving up the pitch as a unit, can push that boundary forward and compress the space in which the attack may operate. This creates the negotiation that gives football much of its shape — attackers timing runs to arrive after the ball is struck rather than before, defenders holding a line and stepping up together, and the whole team of ten outfield players operating within a band perhaps 30 to 40 metres deep rather than spread across the full 100-metre length of the pitch.

The law also creates the sport's most persistent controversy, because it requires an official to judge, at a single instant, the relative positions of players who may be 40 metres apart, while the ball is being struck somewhere else entirely, and to do it in real time. That is a genuinely difficult perceptual task, and it is the reason offside consumes so much of the argument around football, from the shouting on a touchline to the deployment of camera arrays tracking 29 points on each player's body 50 times a second.

The structure of the law is simple once separated into its parts. There is a definition of an offside position, which is purely geometric. There is a separate definition of an offside offence, which requires the player to do something. And there is a list of exemptions.

sections.heading: The Law in Two Parts: Position and Offence
sections.body:
The single most common misunderstanding of Law 11 is the belief that standing in an offside position is against the rules. It is not, and the law says so explicitly: being in an offside position is not, in itself, an offence. An attacker may spend the entire match standing behind the last defender and never once be penalised, provided they never become involved in active play at a moment when they are in that position.

The law therefore has two tests that must both be satisfied before a whistle is blown. The first is positional and purely geometric: at the moment a teammate plays or touches the ball, was the player in an offside position? The second is about involvement: did the player then become involved in active play in one of the specific ways the law lists? Only if both answers are yes has an offence occurred. Assistant referees are trained to think in exactly this order, and the delay you often see before a flag goes up is usually the official waiting to see whether the second condition will be satisfied.

The distinction has real consequences on the pitch. A striker standing offside on the far side of the penalty area while a cross is delivered to a teammate on the near post has not committed an offence, and the goal stands. The same striker, standing in the same place, who ducks under the cross or gestures to draw a defender's attention may well have committed one, because they have interfered with an opponent. Nothing about the geometry changed; only the involvement did.

It also explains why the law needs so much definitional machinery. Once you accept that position alone is insufficient, you must specify exactly what counts as involvement, and the answer is neither obvious nor uncontroversial. Does an offside player who runs toward the ball but does not touch it interfere with play? What if a defender changes course because of that run? What if the offside player is simply in the goalkeeper's eyeline? Each of these was answered by successive rewritings between 1990 and 2013, and the current wording is the accumulated result.

The two-part structure is also why the law can be applied differently by two competent officials without either being wrong in an obvious sense. The positional judgement is factual and, given enough technology, determinable to the centimetre. The involvement judgement contains genuine evaluative terms — clearly obstructing, obvious action, impacts on the ability of an opponent to play the ball — that require a referee to form a view. Technology has largely settled the first question and has not, and probably cannot, settle the second.

sections.heading: What Counts as an Offside Position
sections.body:
The positional test has a precise definition, and each of its elements matters. A player is in an offside position if any part of the head, body or feet is in the opponents' half of the field of play, excluding the halfway line itself, and any part of the head, body or feet is nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent.

Take the elements in turn. The reference to head, body or feet is deliberate and was clarified in the 2016 revision of the Laws: the hands and arms are excluded, for every player including the goalkeeper, because a player cannot legally score or play the ball with them. For the purposes of drawing an offside line, the boundary of the arm is defined as the bottom of the armpit, so a shoulder counts and an elbow does not. This is why technology-assisted decisions are drawn from a knee, a shoulder or a toe rather than from a fingertip.

The phrase any part matters too: it is not the player's centre of mass, nor their feet, nor where they seem to be. If a striker's shoulder is a centimetre beyond the defender's nearest legal body part, they are in an offside position, however absurd that looks. The corollary is that the same test applies to the defender, so the line is drawn from whichever part of the defender is furthest back toward their own goal.

The second-last opponent is the crucial reference, and it is worth stating carefully: the player must be nearer the goal line than at least two opponents. Almost always one of those two is the goalkeeper, so in practice the reference is the last outfield defender. But nothing in the law requires this. If a goalkeeper has come out for a corner, or has rushed from goal and been bypassed, the two relevant opponents may both be outfield players, and the offside line is then drawn from the second-rearmost of them wherever they happen to be.

The ball is the other reference. A player level with or behind the ball is never in an offside position, which is why a player running onto a through-ball played square or backwards is always onside no matter where the defenders are.

Finally, level is onside. If the attacker's furthest-forward legal body part is exactly level with the second-last opponent's rearmost legal body part, they are not in an offside position. The same applies to being level with the ball. This benefit-of-the-doubt provision, introduced in 1990, is a substantive rule and not merely a refereeing courtesy, and technology applies it literally: a rendered overlay showing the two lines touching is an onside verdict.

sections.heading: When a Position Becomes an Offence
sections.body:
A player in an offside position commits an offence only if, at the moment the ball is played or touched by a teammate, they become involved in active play. The law defines three ways this can happen, and their wording repays close reading because almost every disputed offside call in modern football turns on one of them rather than on the geometry.

The first is interfering with play, which the law defines narrowly as playing or touching a ball passed or touched by a teammate. This is the straightforward case: the striker runs onto the through-ball and shoots. Note how limited the definition is — it requires actual contact with the ball. A player who merely runs into space has not interfered with play in this sense.

The second is interfering with an opponent, which is where the judgement lies. The law lists four situations: preventing an opponent from playing or being able to play the ball by clearly obstructing the opponent's line of vision; challenging an opponent for the ball; clearly attempting to play a ball which is close by, when this action impacts on an opponent; and making an obvious action which clearly impacts on the ability of an opponent to play the ball. The recurring qualifiers — clearly, obvious, impacts — are doing deliberate work. A striker standing in an offside position who does nothing is not penalised even if a defender happens to glance at them. A striker who lunges at a ball passing nearby, causing the goalkeeper to hesitate, is. The standard is behavioural and observable, not psychological.

The third is gaining an advantage, which covers rebounds. A player in an offside position who plays a ball that has rebounded or been deflected off a goalpost, the crossbar, a match official or an opponent, or that has come off a deliberate save by any opponent, has gained an advantage and is penalised. So too if they interfere with an opponent after such a rebound. The logic is that the offside player's illegitimate positional advantage was not cancelled by the deflection.

Two further provisions complete the picture. A player in an offside position who receives the ball from an opponent who has deliberately played it, other than a deliberate save, is not committing an offence, because the opponent's decision to play the ball breaks the chain. And a player who commits a foul on an opponent while in an offside position is penalised for whichever offence occurred first, which will normally be the offside if their involvement preceded the contact.

The practical summary is that involvement means touching the ball, physically or visually obstructing an opponent, or capitalising on a rebound.

sections.heading: The Decisive Instant: When the Ball Is Played
sections.body:
Offside is judged at one instant and one instant only: the moment the ball is played or touched by a teammate. Not when the pass arrives. Not when the attacker starts running. Not when the attacker touches it. This single point is the source of more spectator confusion than any other part of the law, because what the eye naturally follows is the arrival of the ball rather than its departure.

The consequence is that an attacker may be many metres beyond the last defender when they receive the ball and be perfectly onside, provided they were level with or behind the second-last opponent at the moment the pass was struck. A striker who begins a run from ten metres behind the defensive line and receives a through-ball fifteen metres beyond it has done nothing wrong; they have simply run faster than the defenders while the ball was in flight. Conversely, an attacker who is standing still when the ball arrives can be offside if they were a shoulder beyond the line when it left the passer's foot.

The law also specifies which instant counts when the touch is not instantaneous. Where a player kicks the ball, the reference is the first point of contact. This matters for a driven pass where the foot stays with the ball for perhaps 10 to 15 milliseconds, and it matters enormously for technology, since a frame captured 20 milliseconds too late can move a sprinting player by around 20 centimetres. A forward running at 9 metres per second covers 9 centimetres every hundredth of a second, so identifying the kick frame precisely is not a detail but the whole problem.

Each new touch resets the judgement. If a teammate plays the ball backwards and a third player then plays it forward, the positions are assessed afresh at that second touch. A player who was offside on the first pass is not permanently tainted; they are simply reassessed. This is why a phase of play with several passes can contain no offside at all even though attackers were repeatedly beyond the line between touches.

An important refinement concerns which teammate's touch counts. The reference is a teammate playing or touching the ball, so a deflection off a teammate can create an offside situation where none existed. If a shot is deflected by a teammate into the path of a player who was in an offside position at the moment of that deflection, an offence has occurred.

The practical instruction that follows for anyone watching, whether from the stand or the touchline, is counterintuitive but reliable: do not watch the player you expect to receive the ball. Watch the passer's foot, and take a mental snapshot of the defensive line at the instant of contact.

sections.heading: The Exemptions: Own Half, Throw-In, Goal Kick and Corner
sections.body:
Four situations exempt a player from offside entirely, and knowing them prevents a large fraction of touchline arguments.

The first is territorial. A player cannot be offside in their own half. The law states that being in the opponents' half is a condition of an offside position, and it explicitly excludes the halfway line itself, so a player standing with one foot on the line and their body behind it is in their own half and cannot be offside. A player whose foot is over the line but whose torso is behind it, however, is in the opponents' half, because any part of the head, body or feet suffices. This exemption dates from 1907 and removes any question about deep-lying players receiving long passes.

The remaining three exempt specific restarts: there is no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from a goal kick, a throw-in or a corner kick. The word directly is essential. The exemption covers the first touch after the restart only. If the throw-in is played to a teammate who then passes forward, ordinary offside applies immediately to that pass. This is why a team can station a striker beyond the last defender at a corner without any risk, and why the same striker must retreat the moment the ball is recycled.

The reasoning behind each is practical rather than principled. Corner kicks and goal kicks are taken from a dead ball at the extremes of the pitch where an offside judgement would be either meaningless or unmanageable; at a corner every attacker in the six-yard box would be technically offside. The throw-in exemption was introduced in 1920, after a period in which offside from throw-ins produced constant stoppages and gave defences an easy weapon.

Two further points complete the picture. A defender who leaves the field of play without the referee's permission, as often happens when a defender is carried past the goal line by momentum, is considered to be on the goal line or touchline for offside purposes until the next stoppage in play. This prevents a defender from stepping off the pitch to put a whole attack offside, an exploit the law closed deliberately. Likewise, an attacking player who has left the field is considered to be on the boundary line, and a player who deliberately leaves the field to avoid being penalised and then returns to interfere may be cautioned.

Finally, offside applies only to the attacking team's own pass. You can never be put offside by an opponent playing the ball to you deliberately, and there is no offside on a drop ball, since the ball is not played by a teammate at the restart.

sections.heading: Rebounds, Saves and Deliberate Play
sections.body:
The single most technical area of Law 11 concerns what happens when the ball reaches an offside-position player indirectly, and it turns on a distinction that referees must make in real time: was the opponent's contact a deliberate play, or was it a save or a deflection?

The rule is asymmetric on purpose. If the ball reaches the offside player because an opponent deliberately played it — a defender attempting an interception, a clearance, a header back toward their own goalkeeper — the offside offence is wiped out. The reasoning is that the defender made a free choice and must take responsibility for its consequences; the attacker's earlier positional advantage is no longer the cause of what happened. But if the ball reaches the offside player off a deliberate save by any opponent, or off a rebound or deflection from a goalpost, the crossbar, a match official or an opponent, the offence stands, and the attacker is penalised for gaining an advantage.

Distinguishing a deliberate play from a deflection or a save proved so contentious that in 2020 IFAB published explicit criteria to guide the judgement. A contact is more likely to count as a deliberate play if the ball travelled from a distance and the player had a clear view of it; if the ball was not moving quickly; if the direction of the ball was not unexpected; if the player had time to coordinate their body movement rather than stretching or lunging; and if a ball on the ground was easier to play than one in the air. A defender who calmly heads a long, looping ball has deliberately played it. A defender who instinctively sticks out a leg at a shot from six metres has not.

The definition of a save is deliberately broad and is not restricted to goalkeepers. A save is when a player stops or attempts to stop a ball which is going, or very close to going, into the goal, with any part of the body except the hands or arms unless that player is the goalkeeper within their own penalty area. So a defender who blocks a goal-bound shot on the line has made a save, and an offside teammate of the shooter who tucks away the rebound is offside. This is the situation that most often produces a disallowed goal that spectators find baffling, since the offside player may have been standing still and doing nothing when the shot was struck.

A further clarification introduced in the early 2020s holds that a deliberate handball by an opponent does not count as deliberate play for these purposes, so an attacker in an offside position who benefits from a defender's handball remains offside. The principle throughout is that the defence should not be punished twice for an attacker's illegal position.

sections.heading: The Punishment and the Restart
sections.body:
When an offside offence is penalised, the restart is an indirect free kick to the defending team, taken from the place where the offence occurred. Both halves of that sentence contain details worth spelling out.

An indirect free kick cannot be scored from directly; the ball must touch another player before entering the goal, and the referee signals this by holding one arm vertically above the head and keeping it there until the kick has been taken and the ball has touched another player or gone out of play. In practice an offside free kick is almost always a routine restart taken quickly by a defender, and the indirect nature rarely matters, though it becomes relevant on the rare occasions when an offside offence occurs close to the offending team's own goal.

The place where the offence occurred means the position of the offending player at the moment the ball was played by their teammate, not where they eventually touched the ball. Since 2013 the law has been explicit that the free kick is taken from that spot even if it is in the offending player's own half, which can produce the unusual sight of an attacking team conceding a free kick deep inside their opponents' territory. If the offence occurs within the defending team's own goal area, the kick may be taken from anywhere within that area.

There is no disciplinary sanction for offside. It is not a caution, it does not accumulate, and there is no such thing as a persistent-offside booking, though a player who leaves the field of play to avoid an offside position and then re-enters to interfere may be cautioned for entering without permission.

When a goal is scored and offside is subsequently detected, the goal is disallowed and play restarts with the indirect free kick from the position of the offence. Where video review is in operation, the check happens automatically as part of the goal-check protocol, since a goal is one of the four categories of decision video assistant referees examine, alongside penalties, direct red cards and mistaken identity. Offside is treated as a factual matter rather than one requiring the clear-and-obvious-error threshold applied to subjective judgements, which is why very marginal offsides are overturned in a way that many spectators feel is disproportionate: on a factual question there is no margin to give.

One consequence of the two-part structure is worth restating here. If the assistant flags and the referee whistles, play stops and the free kick is given. If the assistant judges that the player in an offside position never became involved, no offence has occurred at all, and there is nothing to restart — play simply continues, which is why a goal can legitimately be scored while an opposition player stands well beyond the last defender, apparently offside, doing nothing.

sections.heading: From 1863 to 1925: How the Law Was Built
sections.body:
The offside law is older than almost everything else in football, and its history is a sequence of corrections to abuses. The original Laws of the Game adopted by the newly formed Football Association in December 1863 contained an offside provision far stricter than the modern one: any player ahead of the ball when it was played was out of play and could not touch it. Football was, in effect, a game of dribbling and backing up, close in spirit to the rugby code from which it had just separated, and forward passing was impossible.

The Sheffield rules, developed independently from 1858, were more permissive, and the tension between the codes drove reform. In 1866 the Football Association adopted a requirement that three opponents be between the attacker and the goal line when the ball was played. This is the version that made the passing game possible, and combination play developed rapidly through the 1870s, particularly among Scottish sides, whose passing style eventually displaced the English dribbling game.

A refinement in 1907 established that a player could not be offside in their own half, and in 1920 offside from throw-ins was abolished, both changes reducing stoppages.

The famous reform came in 1925. Under the three-opponent rule, defences had learned to operate a coordinated trap. Newcastle United's full-backs Bill McCracken and Frank Hudspeth are traditionally credited with perfecting it in the years before and after the First World War, stepping up in unison to catch attackers offside so relentlessly that matches became a procession of free kicks. Scoring collapsed and crowds grew restive. The International Football Association Board reduced the requirement from three opponents to two, which is the modern number.

The effect was immediate and enormous. In the English Football League, the 1924-25 season produced roughly 4,700 goals across 1,848 matches, about 2.58 per game. The following season, under the new law, the same number of matches produced roughly 6,370 goals, about 3.45 per game — an increase of around a third in a single summer. The tactical response was equally dramatic. Herbert Chapman, then at Arsenal, pulled the centre-half back from midfield into a purely defensive stopper role between the two full-backs, producing the WM formation that dominated British football for the next thirty years.

That episode is the clearest evidence in the sport's history that the offside law is a tuning parameter for the entire game. Changing it by one player altered goal-scoring rates, formations, player roles and the geometry of the pitch within a season. Every subsequent amendment has been made with that lesson in mind, which is why the Board has preferred clarifications of involvement to further changes in the number of defenders.

sections.heading: 1990 Onward: Level Is Onside and the Modern Game
sections.body:
The second decisive reform came in 1990, when the International Football Association Board determined that a player level with the second-last opponent is onside. Before that, an attacker had to be behind the defender; being exactly level was an offence. The change looks small and was anything but, because it converted every genuinely marginal situation from a decision against the attacker into a decision for them, and because on a defensive line of four players holding position, the difference between level and behind is precisely the margin that a well-timed run exploits.

The same period brought a broader shift in interpretation, encouraged by FIFA's instruction that doubt should favour the attacker. Assistant referees were directed not to flag when they were uncertain, and to allow play to continue where an offside-position player was not involved. In 1995 the wording introduced the notion of a player not interfering with play, which opened the modern era of arguments about involvement rather than geometry.

Successive clarifications followed as that wording proved too vague. In 2005 the Board published definitions of interfering with play, interfering with an opponent and gaining an advantage. In 2013 those definitions were tightened, in particular by specifying that challenging an opponent for the ball and making an obvious action that impacts on an opponent's ability to play it both count as interference. In 2016 the law was restated in terms of head, body or feet, formally excluding the arms. In 2020 the criteria for deliberate play were published.

The cumulative effect of these changes has been to shift football's balance toward attack and toward a compressed, high-tempo game. With level counting as onside and with defences unable to rely on marginal calls, teams pushed their defensive lines higher up the pitch to squeeze the space between the lines, which in turn made the goalkeeper a sweeper obliged to patrol the space behind, and made pace in central defenders a premium attribute. The modern high line and the modern ball-playing goalkeeper are both downstream of an offside law that rewards defenders for stepping up.

A further proposal has been discussed since around 2020, associated with Arsène Wenger in his role as FIFA's head of global football development: that a player should be onside if any part of the body with which they can legally play the ball is level with the second-last defender, rather than offside if any part is beyond. This so-called daylight rule would require clear separation before a flag, eliminating the toenail offsides that technology has made possible. It has been trialled in some competitions but not adopted into the Laws, and whether it will be remains genuinely open.

sections.heading: The Assistant Referee's Job
sections.body:
The offside decision belongs, in the first instance, to the assistant referee patrolling one touchline, and understanding the mechanics of that job explains both why the decision is hard and why officials position themselves as they do.

The assistant's primary instruction is to stay level with the second-last opponent, or with the ball if the ball is nearer the goal line than that opponent. This is not a suggestion but the central discipline of the role, because the only way to judge whether two players are level is to view them along a line perpendicular to the touchline. Viewed from anywhere else, parallax makes the nearer player appear further forward or further back than they are. An assistant standing five metres behind the defensive line will systematically judge attackers to be onside when they are not; standing five metres ahead produces the opposite bias. The consequence is that an assistant referee sprints backwards and forwards along the touchline for ninety minutes with their head turned, attempting to maintain a moving alignment while also watching a ball being struck up to 50 metres away.

The signalling procedure is prescribed. To indicate offside the assistant raises the flag vertically. Once the referee has stopped play, the assistant indicates where on the field the offence occurred by holding the flag at roughly 45 degrees upward for the far side of the pitch, horizontally for the middle third, and at 45 degrees downward for the near side. The flag is raised in the hand nearer the pitch so that the referee sees it clearly.

Since the mid-2000s, and much more strictly since video review arrived, assistants have been instructed to delay the flag in certain situations. If an attacking move is developing into an immediate goalscoring opportunity and the offside judgement is close, the assistant keeps the flag down and allows the phase to complete, raising it only once the ball is dead or the attack has ended. The reasoning is that a goal wrongly disallowed cannot be recovered, whereas a goal wrongly allowed can be reviewed and cancelled. Assistants are simultaneously instructed to flag immediately where there is a clear offside and no imminent goalscoring opportunity, so that play is not allowed to run on pointlessly, and where there is any danger of a serious collision.

This wait-and-see protocol produces a familiar and unloved sequence: an attacker scores, the flag goes up afterwards, and the celebration is retracted. It is not indecision but a deliberate policy, and it is the direct cost of prioritising the correctness of goals over the immediacy of decisions.

The assistant also has responsibilities that compete with offside — the touchline, fouls in their quadrant, substitutions — which is why the offside judgement, though the most scrutinised, is not the only thing they are doing.

sections.heading: Why Human Eyes Get It Wrong
sections.body:
Offside errors are not primarily a matter of competence or attention. They arise from well-documented limits of the visual system, and understanding them is the fairest way to think about officiating.

The first constraint is that the judgement requires attending to two widely separated locations at once. The assistant must register the instant the ball leaves the passer's foot, which may be 30 to 50 metres away in the centre of the pitch, and simultaneously register the relative positions of an attacker and a defender in the near field. Human vision has a narrow region of high acuity — the fovea covers only about two degrees of the visual field — so one of the two locations is necessarily in peripheral vision, where spatial resolution is far poorer. Saccadic eye movements between the two take on the order of 200 milliseconds each, during which a sprinting attacker moves nearly two metres.

The second constraint is the flash-lag effect, a robust perceptual illusion in which a moving object is perceived as being further along its path than a briefly presented stationary reference. Applied to football, this predicts that when an assistant registers the instant of the pass, a running attacker will be perceived as slightly ahead of their true position, biasing judgements toward flagging offside. Researchers including Baldo, Ranvaud and Morya proposed this explanation in a 2002 paper analysing flag errors, and it fits the observed asymmetry that false offside calls outnumber missed ones in several datasets.

The third is optical error from viewing angle.
