In a 2000 paper in Nature, Raoul Oudejans and colleagues argued that even a perfectly positioned assistant suffers a systematic error because the assistant's eye, the attacker and the defender are not collinear in the way the flat two-dimensional analogy assumes; the direction of the error depends on which player is nearer the touchline and on which side of the assistant the pair are situated. Later work by Werner Helsen, Bart Gilis and Matthew Weston, and by Johan Wagemans and colleagues, has produced a picture in which both mechanisms contribute, with disagreement about their relative weight.

The measured error rates are sobering. Analyses of elite tournaments, including a study of all offside decisions at the 2002 World Cup, have reported incorrect judgements in roughly a sixth to a quarter of cases, with error rates rising sharply as the true margin narrows and as the ball travels further. Below about 10 centimetres of separation, unaided human judgement is close to a coin toss, which is the honest reason technology was adopted.

None of this means the naked eye is useless. Assistants get the large majority of clear decisions right, and the errors concentrate in the marginal cases that no human system could resolve. It does mean that criticising an official for missing a 5-centimetre offside is criticising them for not exceeding the limits of the visual system.

sections.heading: VAR and Semi-Automated Offside Technology
sections.body:
Video assistance for offside was written into the Laws of the Game in 2018 and used at that year's World Cup. Under the standard protocol, a video assistant referee checks every goal, and offside is one of the things checked. Because offside position is a factual matter, it is not subject to the clear-and-obvious-error threshold that applies to subjective decisions; if the lines show the attacker beyond the defender, the goal is cancelled regardless of the margin.

The manual method required an operator to identify the frame in which the ball was struck, then place two virtual lines on a calibrated three-dimensional model of the pitch, one at the defender's rearmost legal body part and one at the attacker's foremost. Both steps introduce error. Broadcast cameras typically capture 50 frames per second, so the true kick moment can fall up to 20 milliseconds from the nearest frame, during which a fast attacker moves perhaps 15 to 20 centimetres. Line placement is a human judgement about which pixel corresponds to a shoulder. The process could take three or four minutes, which was itself corrosive to the game's rhythm, and several leagues responded by widening the drawn lines to represent a tolerance band — the English Premier League adopted thicker lines for the 2020-21 season — rather than pretending to a precision the method did not have.

Semi-automated offside technology addressed both problems. Deployed at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and in the UEFA Champions League from the 2022-23 season, it uses a dozen dedicated tracking cameras mounted under the stadium roof, following 29 data points on each player's body 50 times a second, and combines this with an inertial measurement unit inside the match ball transmitting at 500 times a second, which identifies the exact instant of the kick far more precisely than video frames allow. Software constructs the offside line automatically, alerts the video officials when a player is beyond it, and generates a three-dimensional animation for the stadium screens and broadcasters. The video assistant still validates the automatic decision, which is why the system is semi-automated rather than automatic. Typical decision times fell from minutes to tens of seconds.

Adoption has been uneven. Several major leagues moved more slowly, with the Premier League introducing the technology in April 2025 after delays. Costs, stadium fitting and integration with existing broadcast infrastructure are the practical obstacles.

Two honest caveats remain. The technology settles the geometry but not the involvement question, which is still a human judgement about interference. And it has made visible a class of offsides — an armpit, a heel, a shin — that no observer could ever have detected, which is why proposals to introduce a deliberate margin, such as requiring visible daylight between attacker and defender, continue to be debated rather than dismissed.

sections.heading: Defending: The Offside Trap and the High Line
sections.body:
From the defending team's point of view, offside is a weapon, and using it well is one of the most demanding pieces of coordination in the sport.

The basic mechanism is the flat back line. Four defenders, occasionally three or five, hold a common depth across the pitch and move up and down together. Every metre the line advances is a metre of space taken away from the attackers behind it, and because the offside boundary is defined by the second-last opponent, the line effectively carries the boundary with it. A team defending with its line on the halfway line compresses the whole game into the opponents' half, which is what modern pressing sides seek: with the goalkeeper positioned 15 to 20 metres off the goal line as a sweeper, the ten outfield players can occupy a band perhaps 30 metres deep instead of 60.

The trap proper is the deliberate, synchronised step forward at the moment an opponent prepares to pass, timed so that the intended receiver is left beyond the line as the ball is struck. Executed well it turns a promising attack into a free kick. The demands are severe. The step must be simultaneous, because a single defender who is a metre slow keeps everyone onside — this is the single most common cause of failure, and it is why one poorly positioned centre-back can nullify an entire team's defensive scheme. It must be triggered by a shared cue, normally the passer's body shape as they load the pass, and normally called by one designated organiser, historically the central defender. And it must not be attempted when the passer has the ball under close control and can simply dribble through the vacated space.

The risks are proportionate. A trap that fails leaves an attacker running unopposed at the goalkeeper. A chipped or lofted pass over the stepping line is harder to time. A quickly taken free kick can catch the line before it has organised. And any deflection or second ball behind the line arrives in an area no defender occupies.

There is also a strategic cost that has grown as the law has been interpreted more favourably to attackers. Against a side with genuinely fast forwards, a high line invites the one pass that ends the match, and coaches must weigh compression against exposure. The historical arc runs from Newcastle United's ruthless pre-1925 trap, through Arsenal's back four under George Graham in the late 1980s, to the modern pressing systems associated with Marcelo Bielsa, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola, in which the offside line is less a trap than a permanent structural choice sustained by pressing the ball hard enough that accurate passes behind it are rare.

sections.heading: Attacking: Beating the Line Legally
sections.body:
For an attacker, offside is a timing discipline, and the skills involved are as coachable as shooting or passing. The governing insight is that the law fixes position at the instant of the pass and says nothing about what happens afterwards, so the objective is to be moving fast but still level when the ball is struck.

The first technique is the delayed run. A forward who sets off early is offside; one who sets off late arrives after the defence has recovered. The solution is to start from a position two or three metres behind the line and to accelerate into the run as the passer loads their kicking foot, so that maximum speed is reached just after the ball leaves. This requires reading the passer rather than the ball, and it is why great forwards appear to move before the pass exists.

The second is the curved or bent run. A run made straight at the goal crosses the offside line at right angles, giving the narrowest possible margin for error and the worst possible viewing angle for the assistant. A run that starts wide, arcs back toward the halfway line and then bends forward keeps the attacker onside for longer, lets them time their crossing of the line, and arrives with momentum across the defender rather than into their back. Coaches teach it as running the line from the outside in.

The third is the double movement: a short step toward the ball to draw the defender forward, followed by a spin in behind. The half-yard gained is often enough, because a defender who has committed forward cannot restore the line.

The fourth is exploiting the reference points. Since offside is measured against the second-last opponent, an attacker positioned level with a full-back who has pushed high on the far side may be onside even while apparently well beyond the nearest defenders. Attackers are taught to know where the deepest two opponents are, not merely the nearest one. Similarly, since a player level with or behind the ball is never in an offside position, running from deep onto a square or cut-back pass is always safe, which is why the pull-back from the byline is a staple of modern attacking play.

The fifth is passive use of the position. An attacker who is offside and knows it should stand still and visibly disengage, because doing nothing is not an offence, and a teammate arriving onside can then score. Conversely, an attacker who is unsure should assume they are offside and take care not to touch the ball or obstruct a defender.

The final and most reliable technique is the deliberate stay-behind. A forward who consciously holds a position a stride behind the line surrenders a little space in exchange for eliminating the risk entirely, and against a well-drilled trap that trade is often correct.

sections.heading: Misconceptions, Edge Cases and Judging It Yourself
sections.body:
Several beliefs about offside are widely held and simply wrong, and clearing them away is most of what a spectator needs. It is not offside to be in an offside position; involvement is required. It is not offside to be beyond the last defender when the ball arrives; only the moment it was played matters. It is not offside if you are level. There is no offside from a throw-in, a goal kick or a corner, but only for the first touch. You cannot be offside in your own half. You cannot be offside from a pass played by an opponent. And offside is not a bookable offence.

Some edge cases are worth knowing. A player in an offside position who blocks the goalkeeper's line of sight when a shot is taken can be penalised without touching the ball, because obstructing vision counts as interfering with an opponent. A goalkeeper is not automatically one of the two relevant opponents, so if the keeper has advanced, the line is drawn from the second-rearmost outfielder. A defender lying injured off the pitch behind the goal line is treated as being on the goal line, so they still count. Where two attackers challenge for the same ball, only the one who actually becomes involved is penalised. And a deflection off a teammate creates a fresh offside judgement at the instant of that deflection, which is why goals are occasionally disallowed for an offside no one saw coming.

Judging it yourself is largely a matter of discipline about where you look and honesty about what you cannot see. Anyone far from the line of the defence has a viewing angle that makes marginal calls meaningless, and the correct conclusion is then that you do not know.
steps: Before the pass, locate the second-rearmost opponent, which usually means the last outfield defender rather than the goalkeeper, and note where the flat line across the pitch sits.
Watch the passer's kicking foot, not the intended receiver, because the only instant that matters is first contact with the ball.
At that instant, take a mental snapshot: is any part of the attacker's head, body or feet nearer the goal line than both the ball and that second-rearmost opponent? Ignore arms entirely.
If they are level, or behind, or in their own half, or behind the ball, stop — there is no offside position and nothing further to judge.
If they were beyond, ask whether the restart was a throw-in, goal kick or corner, since a first touch directly from any of those cannot be an offence.

Then ask what the player actually did: touched the ball, challenged or blocked an opponent, obstructed the goalkeeper's view, or made an obvious action affecting a defender. If none of these, no offence has occurred.
If the ball reached them indirectly, decide whether the opponent's contact was a calm deliberate play, which wipes out the offence, or a save, deflection or rebound, which does not.
Check your own viewing angle honestly: unless you are close to level with the defensive line, treat any margin under about half a metre as genuinely undecidable.
